channel.title: Acme: Tech News
channel.description: Articles about software, publishing and the open web.

item.title: Podcast trade group backs migration safeguards and measurement standards
item.description: The Podcast Professionals Association endorsed the Podcast Migration Code of Practice and called for transparent, consistent audience measurement. It also urged player developers to weigh the economic effects of easier ad skipping while preserving listener choice—a useful attempt to put shared rules around an interoperable medium.

item.title: Wall Street Journal shifts to a bot whitelist
item.description: Dow Jones now disallows bots by default across the Wall Street Journal, Barron’s and MarketWatch, permitting selected crawlers through a whitelist. Nieman Lab reports that publishers are using robots.txt restrictions to reduce bandwidth costs, seek licensing agreements and respond to falling human referrals.

item.title: W3C advances WebAssembly 3.0 candidate drafts
item.description: The W3C published another Candidate Recommendation Draft of the WebAssembly core specification on November 24. The continuing 3.0 work matters to independent web developers because it strengthens a portable, open low-level code format that can run across browsers and other interoperable environments.

item.title: Small local news sites find traffic gains in newsletters, obits and service journalism
item.description: Nieman Lab’s latest ranking of local for-profit news sites shows that useful, distinctive coverage can still travel. Big gainers drew readers through obituary follow-ups, newsletter distribution and service pieces such as a guide to the 690-mile World’s Longest Yard Sale—practical evidence that small publishers can win attention without chasing national scale.

item.title: WebKit adds an interface for Global Privacy Control
item.description: WebKit now lets apps built with WKWebView or WebPage for SwiftUI expose a user setting for Global Privacy Control, the emerging signal for opting out of data sale, sharing and cross-context targeted advertising. The change gives independent browser and app developers a standards-based privacy control across Apple’s current operating systems.

item.title: San Jose Earthquakes announce a change of ownership
item.description: Heath Freeman will acquire the San Jose Earthquakes and PayPal Park from John Fisher and partners after unanimous approval by Major League Soccer’s Board of Governors. The deal, whose financial terms were not disclosed, is expected to close in the coming weeks and gives a founding MLS club new stewardship in Silicon Valley.

item.title: A one-person tech newsroom reaches an $800,000 run rate
item.description: Inc. profiles Alex Konrad’s bootstrapped Upstarts Media, a newsletter, podcast and events business launched after he left Forbes. With about 13,000 newsletter subscribers, roughly 1,000 paying readers and sponsorships supplying most revenue, the operation is on pace for about $800,000 this year—but its dependence on one reporter is also its central risk.

item.title: Firefox cuts Android app-link startup time by about 20 percent
item.description: Mozilla says Firefox for Android now opens links from other apps about 20% faster than in January. The browser begins network work earlier, delays most extension startup and replaces an animated splash screen. On a Samsung A55 reference phone, one news-site launch fell from 2,054 milliseconds to 1,597.

item.title: Firefox reduces the identifying details exposed to fingerprinting scripts
item.description: Mozilla’s study of measurements from nearly 25 million Firefox users found that protecting a small set of browser features can sharply weaken fingerprinting. Firefox now obscures details such as exact processor counts and desktop layout information, while Mozilla published its methods and a browser test suite for independent scrutiny.

item.title: AT Protocol prepares permissioned Spaces for a December 1 beta
item.description: AT Protocol says its Spaces extension will enter public beta December 1, adding permissioned data for private groups, newsletters and other shared applications. Reference servers will gain support through an update, while new documentation and an SDK aim to let independent developers build interoperable social tools for millions of accounts.

item.title: WordPress.com documents an open-feed path to podcast distribution
item.description: WordPress.com’s newly reviewed podcast guide shows how even a free site can publish a submission-ready RSS feed while hosting audio elsewhere, then distribute episodes to Apple, Spotify, YouTube Music, Pocket Casts and Podcast Index. It is a practical example of the open feed remaining the portable spine beneath many listening apps.

item.title: NPR makes rebuilding its app central to its next strategy
item.description: NPR’s 2027–2029 plan calls for a service-first, app-first destination, targeting five million weekly platform users and a 40 million monthly digital audience by 2029. The shift reflects a public media network trying to preserve radio while building direct digital relationships and giving member stations a better place in the product.

item.title: NewsBlur rebuilds its mobile web reader
item.description: NewsBlur replaced its long-neglected mobile site with a responsive version of the desktop reader. The rewrite shares one codebase, adds touch-friendly layouts and swipe gestures, respects the browser back button, and makes the feed list paint immediately—useful progress for an independent, web-native RSS reader.

item.title: Feeder counts more than 300,000 recently active RSS feeds
item.description: Feeder’s newly updated answer to “Is RSS dead?” uses its own index as evidence: more than 300,000 followed feeds published something in the previous 30 days. The article also maps RSS’s quiet infrastructure role across publishers and podcast apps, a measurable counterpoint to recurring declarations that the format has vanished.

item.title: Public media faces a choice beyond simply restoring federal funds
item.description: With a new Congress arriving January 3 after the Corporation for Public Broadcasting’s dissolution, Nieman Lab examines whether lawmakers should recreate the old system or build something more local and democratic. Proposals include public media centers governed by communities rather than another return to the previous structure.
